newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Rouble policy seen little changed in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Rouble policy seen little changed in 1997.

text.p: Russia is likely to continue its current exchange rate policy in 1997 after stabilising the rouble rate this year, dealers said.

"From the point of view of financial stabilisation, the policy was definitely a success. They managed to cope with the main problem about the rouble, its unpredictable jumps," United Investment Bank chief dealer Alexander Suchkov said.

The central bank currently sets a corridor, or upper and lower limits for the rouble. Since July this year there have been daily preset limits, allowing a gentle devaluation of the rouble, similar to a crawling peg.
Within these 600-point ranges, the central bank also sets a narrower range, announced every day, of 10-30 points for its trading in the interbank market.
The rouble has never broken through either of these ranges.
Dealers said they saw no reasons for the central bank to greatly modify rouble policy in 1997, given the positive influence of the stable rouble on the budget.
The central bank is likely to announce details of the new system next week, a month before the current regime expires.
Central bank officials say major changes in regulating the rouble are unlikely.
Deputy chairman Alexander Potyomkin said on Thursday there was no reason to change the rouble corridor policy much.
"The current policy will be continued in 1997, only the band of the fluctuation rate will be changed," he said.
The annual inflation rate was expected to fall to 12 percent in 1997 from around 25 percent in 1996, Potyomkin said.
"Changes in the current ranges will be based on this and change of local prices," Potyomkin said.
The latest draft of the budget submitted to parliament by the government assumes an average exchange rate in 1997 of 5,750 roubles a dollar.
The rouble is now quoted at around 5,500 per dollar.
Aljba Alliance Bank chief dealer Dmitry Slobodnik said the central bank could allow broader fluctuations next year to cut its spending of dollars of to keep the rouble under control.

"Banks have stopped thinking about the rouble/dollar market as one for investments or speculations. They mainly turn to it if they need roubles to buy government bonds or to return their assets into dollars," he said.
Suchkov said the rate of decline and limits of the crawling corridor could change.
"Russia has achieved its aim of depreciating the rouble in line with the inflation rate. It has also relieved pressure on the budget, pushing down yields of the government bonds," he said.
Yields of Russia Treasury bills fallen to around 40 percent from 80 percent in January mainly due to active non-resident buying, and are likely to fall further in future.
